hints: Start by thinking about what has to happen first in any nervous response - what is there in the environment that the nervous system needs to pick up?
Think about energy forms - light, pressure, chemicals are not electrical, but neurones communicate electrically. What job must the receptor do to link the two?
Once that electrical change is made, what is it called and where does it have to go next to start the nervous pathway?
walkthrough:
Detecting a Change in the Environment**
Think of receptor cells as the lookouts. They detect a change in stimulus such as light, heat, sound, touch, pressure, pain or chemicals. Without this first detection, no nervous impulse can begin.

Transduction Into Electrical Energy**
Stimulus energy cannot travel along a neurone. The receptor acts as a transducer, converting stimulus energy into electrical energy. This produces a small depolarisation called a generator or receptor potential.

Starting the Sensory Pathway**
If that generator potential is large enough it will trigger an action potential that is passed to and along a sensory neurone toward the CNS. So the sequence is detect - transduce - initiate impulse.

Final answer: Detect and respond to a change in stimulus, e.g. light, sound, touch, pressure, chemicals; act as transducers converting stimulus energy into electrical energy as a generator / receptor potential; which passes an impulse to / along a sensory neurone.

hints: Look at the shape of the curve - C is the steep rise from about -50 mV to +40 mV, D is the steep fall, E is the flat resting line at -70 mV. Which ion movement causes up and which causes down?
Remember depolarisation is $Na^+$ rushing in and repolarisation is $K^+$ rushing out. Match those to C and D.
Remember the $Na^+/K^+$ pump works all the time to restore and maintain gradients, especially during repolarisation and at rest. Which letters could that cover?
walkthrough:
Reading C - The Rising Phase**
At C the membrane potential shoots up from threshold at about -50 mV to +40 mV. That can only happen by rapid influx of $Na^+$ through open voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels, causing depolarisation.

Reading D - The Falling Phase**
At D the potential falls rapidly back down. That is repolarisation caused by voltage-gated $K^+$ channels opening and $K^+$ moving out, while $Na^+$ channels close. The $Na^+/K^+$ pump is also helping restore gradients here.

Reading E - The Resting State**
At E the trace is flat at about -70 mV, the resting potential. No voltage-gated channels are open, but the $Na^+/K^+$ pump continues to operate to maintain the $Na^+$ and $K^+$ gradients. So pump = C or D and E, $Na^+$ channels = C, $K^+$ channels = D.
Final answer: The $Na^+/K^+$ pump is operating: C or D and E; The voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels are open: C; The voltage-gated $K^+$ channels are open: D.

hints: Compare the size of the small bump after stimulus A with the dashed threshold line at about -50 mV. Did A reach it?
Think about the name for the small graded depolarisation in a receptor and the all-or-nothing rule for firing an action potential.
walkthrough:
A Small Graded Response vs Threshold**
Stimulus A causes only a small depolarisation from -70 mV to about -60 mV. The dashed threshold line is at about -50 mV, so this generator potential stays below threshold.

All-or-Nothing Firing**
An action potential only fires if threshold is reached to open enough voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels. Stimulus A fails, so the membrane returns to rest. Stimulus B is stronger, depolarises to threshold, opens $Na^+$ channels and triggers the full action potential to +40 mV.

Final answer: Stimulus A produced only a small generator / receptor potential; threshold potential was not reached / exceeded, so no action potential fired, whereas stimulus B depolarised the membrane to threshold.

hints: During the refractory period the membrane cannot be re-stimulated immediately - what does that mean for how close together two action potentials can be?
If the region just behind a moving action potential is still refractory, in which direction can the impulse go next?
walkthrough:
Limiting Frequency**
In the refractory period voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels are closed / inactivated and the membrane is hyperpolarised, so a new action potential cannot start at once. This sets a minimum time between impulses and so limits maximum frequency, which allows stimulus intensity to be coded by frequency.

Ensuring One-Way Flow**
The region of axon just behind the advancing action potential is refractory, so it cannot be depolarised backwards. The local circuit can therefore only depolarise the next resting region ahead, so impulses travel in one direction.
Final answer: Limits / controls the maximum frequency of action potentials / impulses; ensures action potentials travel in one direction only.

hints: Start with what myelin does - it insulates most of the axon so ions cannot cross there. Where are the only places with voltage-gated channels?
Think about charge spreading sideways inside the axon from an action potential region to the next excitable patch - what is this local flow called?
What happens when that spread of positive charge reaches the next node and opens its channels?
Put a name to this jumping from node to node and think why it is fast and one-way.
walkthrough:
Insulation by Myelin**
Schwann cells form the myelin sheath which is impermeable to $Na^+$ and $K^+$ and insulates the axon. Voltage-gated channels are concentrated only at gaps called nodes of Ranvier. So depolarisation and action potentials can only occur at nodes.

Local Circuits Ahead**
An action potential at one node makes that region positive inside. $Na^+$ ions are repelled sideways inside the axon, setting up a local circuit with current flowing from the positive active region to the negative resting region ahead. Myelin lengthens these local circuits.

Regeneration at the Next Node**
When this positive charge reaches the next node it depolarises it to threshold, opening its voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels. $Na^+$ rushes in and a new full-size action potential is generated there.

Saltatory Conduction**
The action potential appears to jump from node to node. This is saltatory conduction. It is much faster than continuous conduction because fewer regions need depolarising, and it remains one-way because the previous node is refractory.

Final answer: Myelin sheath insulates axon preventing ion movement except at nodes of Ranvier; local circuit of ions flows from positive to negative region ahead; opens voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels at next node; causing a new action potential / depolarisation there, i.e. saltatory conduction, giving fast one-way transmission.
